Black-browed albatross chicks hatch after a prolonged incubation period, with eggs typically maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during the later stages of development, a thermal regime that influences the total age at birth. Field records indicate that the incubation period averages 72.1 days [ab = 72.1 days], a duration consistent with the extended embryonic development observed among other large procellariiform seabirds at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are brooded intensively by both parents, and their initial body mass at emergence is relatively modest. The wet weight at birth has been recorded at approximately 175.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 175.8 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves that sustain the chick during its first few days before regular parental provisioning begins. This neonatal mass is somewhat lower than that reported for the congeneric wandering albatross, a difference likely attributable to the more streamlined life-history strategy of the smaller-bodied Black-browed species.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the fledging stage is achieved at 120 days since birth [tx = 120 days since birth]. This milestone, marking the first flight achievement and the growing juvenile's departure from the nest, represents a critical transition toward nutritional independence. The 120-day period is relatively abbreviated compared to some of the larger albatross species, which can require up to 270 days before fledging. After fledging, the juvenile birds enter a prolonged sub-adult phase during which they return to sea and refine their foraging skills, but do not engage in reproductive activities. Sexual maturation, defined by the initiation of fully functional gametogenesis and gonadal swelling, is attained considerably later in life, with puberty occurring at 360 days since birth [tp = 360 days since birth] under these same thermal conditions, a timing that allows for substantial somatic growth before the energetic demands of reproduction begin at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].

Eventually, the time since birth at first brood marks the onset of successful reproduction, and for the Black-browed albatross this event is typically deferred until 8 years after hatching [tR = 8 years after hatching] under the thermal regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This exceptionally delayed first reproduction is a hallmark of the species' slow life-history pace, with young birds spending years prospecting for mates and suitable nesting territories on remote subantarctic islands. Maximum reproductive output is limited by this extended juvenile period and by the constraints of a single-egg clutch. Females generally produce only one egg per breeding event [N_R_i = one egg per breeding event], and that single egg is laid annually during the austral summer, resulting in a clutch frequency of one nesting attempt per year [F_R_i = one nesting attempt per year]. This low annual reproductive rate corresponds to a maximum reproductive output of one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year], underscoring the vulnerability of the population to even modest increases in adult mortality.

Sexual size dimorphism is a notable feature of this species, with adult males attaining a substantially larger ultimate wet weight than females. The ultimate wet weight for females is 3170 grams [Wwi = 3170 grams], while the ultimate wet weight for males reaches 3710 grams [Wwi = 3710 grams], a difference of over 500 grams that is among the more pronounced in the genus Thalassarche. This pronounced dimorphism likely reflects divergent selective pressures: larger body size in males may confer advantages in competitive interactions over nest sites and during courtship displays, whereas the smaller female body mass may facilitate more efficient flight during the energetically demanding incubation and chick-provisioning periods. The maximum recorded longevity for the Black-browed albatross, based on long-term banding studies, is 44 years [am = 44 years] when individuals are subject to the thermal conditions of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Such an extended lifespan is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in a single, well-provisioned offspring each year and whose population dynamics are consequently more sensitive to changes in adult survival than to fluctuations in annual breeding success.

Several life-history adaptations buffer the population against periodic environmental stochasticity, including the extended juvenile phase and the production of a single egg per annual nesting attempt [Ri = single egg per annual nesting attempt]. Studies of marked populations at South Georgia and the Falkland Islands indicate that individuals that survive to reach reproductive age often breed successfully for two decades or more, gradually increasing their proficiency at chick rearing. The combination of high adult survival, late maturity, and low annual fecundity places the Black-browed albatross squarely at the slow end of the life-history continuum, a strategy that has proven successful in the stable, though seasonally productive, Southern Ocean environments they inhabit.
